fields.apa_citation: Gatersleben, B., & Andrews, M. (2013). When walking in nature is not restorative-The role of prospect and refuge. Health & Place, 20, 91-101.
fields.main_conclusion: Natural environments high in prospect (clear field of vision) and low in refuge (few hiding places) are more perceived and actually restorative -- improving mood, attention, and reducing heart rate -- than natural environments low in prospect and high in refuge, which can instead increase stress and attention fatigue.
independent_variables: Prospect-refuge level of the natural environment (low / medium / high prospect, inversely varying refuge)
Setting (laboratory simulation vs. real outdoor field walk), in Study 2
dependent_variables: Affective states (positive affect, attentiveness, fear arousal, sadness, anger/aggression via ZIPERS)
Attention (Necker Cube Pattern Control Task reversals)
fields.construct_pair: Prospect-refuge structure of a natural environment -> Restoration (perceived and actual: mood, attention, heart rate)
fields.stimulus_description: In Study 1, respondents viewed a slideshow of 12 sequential photographs (preceded by a short descriptive narrative) depicting a walk through a country park, manipulated to be low, medium, or high in prospect-refuge. In Study 2, respondents either walked real paths through a low- or high-prospect-refuge section of the same country park, or viewed first-person video recordings of the same walks projected in a laboratory.
fields.methods_surface_summary: Study 1 was a between-subjects online survey (N=269) with three prospect-refuge slideshow conditions, measuring perceived danger, fear, and restoration via one-way ANOVAs, planned contrasts, and mediation analyses. Study 2 used a mixed within/between-subjects design (17 field participants, 17 lab participants) comparing pre/post-walk change scores on affect, attention, and heart rate across high vs. low prospect-refuge walks and field vs. lab settings, analyzed with ANOVA and Tukey post hoc tests.
measurement_inventory: A&D UA-767 digital blood pressure/heart rate monitor (heart rate only used)
Manipulation-check items for prospect, accessibility, and hiding places

notes.sample_n: Paper reports two studies: Study 1 N=269 (online survey), Study 2 N=17 field + 17 lab = 34. Total across studies = 303. Took the sum since the paper is one article with two linked experiments and no single 'main' study is designated; this is an aggregation choice, not a number printed anywhere as a single total.
notes.p_value: Many p-values are reported throughout; selected p<.001 as representative of the strongest/most central reported finding (e.g., perceived restoration difference across prospect-refuge conditions in Study 1, F(2,266)=36.35, p<.001).
notes.effect_size: Multiple Cohen's d values are reported for different sub-comparisons (ranging roughly d=0.26 to d=1.94); selected d=1.24, the largest contrast in Study 1's perceived-restoration effect (low vs. high prospect-refuge), as representative of the central prospect-refuge -> restoration relationship. This is a judgment call given the paper reports no single overall effect size.
notes.direction: High prospect/low refuge consistently associated with more restoration (higher positive affect, attentiveness, lower fear/sadness/anger, greater heart-rate reduction) than low prospect/high refuge, across both studies.
